move: Insists the Just/Expedient distinction is real and the most sacred part of morality while simultaneously disputing any standard of justice not grounded on utility, recasting justice as a name for a class of moral rules.
Analyses duty and injustice through the idea of penal sanction and exactability rather than taking a position on whether justice is objective or conventional.

Reduces justice to those moral requirements highest in social utility, admits particular cases override them, and attributes justice's apparent indefeasibility to a 'useful accommodation of language'.

Exhibits the conflicting conceptions of just punishment — lex talionis and proportionality to moral guilt versus minimum sufficient deterrence — to show no single standard of justice commands agreement.

Analyses the extension of justice beyond law by arguing that calling conduct unjust always carries the lingering idea that it ought to be compelled or punished, without settling the objectivity question.

Gives a genealogy in which the primitive element of justice was conformity to law, then notes Greeks and Romans recognised bad laws, so injustice came to attach to violations of laws that ought to exist.

Identifies justice as each part doing its own business, the same form in state and individual, evidenced by the just man's reliability against theft, sacrilege, and broken oaths, and treats it as a primary form discovered rather than stipulated.
Marks justice off from the rest of morality by the jurists' distinction between perfect and imperfect obligation, tying justice to a correlative personal right, without addressing conventionality.

Argues that if justice were a self-evident standard per se the 'internal oracle' would not be so ambiguous, citing fierce disagreement across nations and within one mind among many non-coinciding maxims chosen by personal predilection.
Against the thesis that injustice is stronger, identifies justice with wisdom and virtue and presses whether even a state's power to enslave others can be exercised without justice.

Reports the received account that justice arose from laws and mutual covenants adopted as a compromise by those unable to do injustice with impunity, making it a tolerated lesser evil rather than a good.

Separates the origin of the justice-feeling from its binding force and poses, without answering, whether the reality behind the feeling is intrinsically peculiar or merely a combination of other qualities.
